program.name: SpaceX Starship
program.description: The SpaceX Starship is a fully reusable super heavy-lift launch vehicle under development by SpaceX since 2012, as a self-funded private spaceflight project.  The second stage of the Starship — is designed as a long-duration cargo and passenger-carrying spacecraft. It is expected to be initially used without any booster stage at all, as part of an extensive development program to prove out launch-and-landing and iterate on a variety of design details, particularly with respect to the vehicle's atmospheric reentry.

launcher.details: Fourth Block 3 Super Heavy booster to fly with various enhancements including Raptor 3 engines, integrated interstage and 3 grid fins instead of 4 used. To be used on the 15th Starship flight test, the 2nd Starship flight to deploy satellites into stable Low Earth Orbit. It is the first Starship V3 booster to attempt landing back on its launch pad.

landing.description: The Super Heavy Booster 22 did not attempt a return back to the launch site at Starbase and splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico instead, due to an abort triggered before landing burn.

location.name: SpaceX Starbase, TX, USA
location.description: Starbase is an industrial complex for Starship rockets and the headquarters of the American aerospace manufacturer company SpaceX. Starbase is composed of a spaceport near the Gulf of Mexico, a production facility at the Boca Chica village, and a small structure test site along the Texas State Highway 4.

mission.name: Starlink Group 31-2 (Starship Flight 15)
mission.description:
15th test flight of the two-stage Starship launch vehicle and 4th flight of Starship V3. Second Starship flight to deploy satellites (a group of Starlink satellites known as Starlink Group 31-2) into stable Low Earth Orbit and first ever to attempt returning the Starship 2nd stage back to the launch site.

The ship is expected to fly at an altitude approximately 275 km above Earth and complete approximately 14 orbits around the planet for more than 22 hours, with the ship expected to attempt returning back to Starbase, Texas on its launch pad by pad arms catching.

The booster’s primary test objective on Flight 15 will be executing a successful launch, ascent, stage separation, boostback burn, and landing by pad arms catching. This will also be the 1st Starship V3 booster to attempt returning to its launch site.

Starship will deliver 26 Starlink V3 satellites to orbit for the second time, which aim to greatly expand the network's capacity and user speeds. Each Starlink V3 satellite will add 1 Tbps of capacity to the constellation. 3 of the satellites have been modified with a suite of cameras to scan Starship’s heatshield and transmit imagery down to operators.

vidURLs.description:
Watch live as SpaceX launches its revolutionary Starship launcher into orbit with plans to catch both the booster and ship back at the launch site. Liftoff of the Version 3 integrated Starship vehicle from Starbase in Texas is scheduled during a launch window that opens at 4:45 p.m. CST / 5:45 p.m. EST / 2245 UTC on Friday, Nov. 13.

Flight 15 will use the Ship 42 upper stage and Booster 22 for the first stage Super Heavy booster. SpaceX plans to deploy 26 Starlink Version 3 satellites from the ship. 

If all goes according to plan the Ship will remain in orbit for 22.5 hours, before returning to Starbase and a catch by the launch pad 'chopstick' arms. Super Heavy booster will also return to the pad about 6.5 minutes after launch.

vidURLs.description:
SpaceX is targeting Starship Flight 15 NET Friday, November 13, 2026 at 4:45 p.m. CT (22:45 UTC), with a 75-minute window. This will be the FIRST attempt to catch both stages of Starship, with Ship 42 and Booster 22, carrying 26 Starlink V3 satellites on a roughly 22.5-hour mission of about 14 orbits at around 275 km. 

Booster 22 will return to the tower for the first-ever catch of a V3 Super Heavy about 6.5 minutes after liftoff. 

If all goes well Ship 42 will come back to Starbase for the first-ever Ship catch around 3:17 p.m. CT on Saturday, which would make it the first fully recovered orbital rocket in history and a huge step toward rapid, full reuse.
